Did Jesus Really Exist in History? A Date Stamp Left by His Enemies
Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea (Luke 3:1)

Brothers and sisters, dear friends, peace to you! Let me start with a question. How do you know your great-grandfather really lived? You probably never met him. Maybe you have a yellowed photograph, a family genealogy, a line in the household registration office. And there is one more kind of evidence that is even more interesting: a neighbor who once took him to court and left behind a complaint in which he is run down as worthless.

Strangely enough, that complaint may be more convincing than the genealogy. A genealogy may want to paint the ancestors in a good light, but a complaint has no such motive. It cannot prove that your great-grandfather was a good man, but it is enough to prove that such a man existed.

Today we walk into the first gallery of Jesus Hall, and we are going to ask a question that many friends have thought about but felt too embarrassed to ask: Was there really a man called Jesus in history? Or did the church make it all up?

Let me say something up front. I am not going to tell you today that “history has proved Jesus is God.” History cannot do that. Today we answer only a smaller question: did He exist or not? But this small question opens a very big door.
1. The line written by His enemies
A Roman senator who looked down on Christians

Let us go back to about AD 116. There was a Roman senator named Tacitus, one of the foremost historians of his day, and he was writing his Annals. When he came to the great fire of Rome in AD 64, he mentioned that the emperor Nero, to turn aside the rumors, pinned the blame on the Christians and punished them with terrible cruelty.

Tacitus had no kind words for Christians. He called their faith a harmful superstition. But to explain to his readers who these people were, he added one sentence in passing: the name came from Christ, who was put to death by Pilate in the reign of Tiberius.

Think about the tone of that sentence, brothers and sisters. It is like us writing a report and adding a footnote: “The leader of this bunch was dealt with years ago.” He had no wish at all to testify for Jesus. Yet two thousand years later, that one line has become a date stamp from an outsider: the person, the emperor and the governor all line up.

Scholars almost all believe this passage came from Tacitus’ own hand. To be honest, we should also say that he wrote more than eighty years after Jesus died, and scholars are still arguing about where his information came from. It may simply have been what everybody knew at the time. So it cannot prove very much, but it is enough to show one thing: even the upper class of Rome knew there had been such a man, and that this was how he was put to death.
A Jewish historian and a governor at his wits’ end

The second witness is the Jewish historian Josephus, who finished his Antiquities of the Jews in AD 93 or 94. In it he records that the high priest Ananus had a man named James put to death. Lest his readers be confused, Josephus makes a point of explaining that this was “the brother of Jesus,” and that this Jesus “was called Christ.”

Scholars accept this passage almost without exception. The same book has another, much more famous passage that describes Jesus directly, saying He did wonders, was crucified and rose on the third day. Here we must be careful. Most scholars believe Josephus did write something there, but that later Christian copyists added words such as “he was the Christ.” A minority think the whole passage was inserted by others. So, brothers and sisters, when you share the gospel, please do not use this passage as iron-clad proof. If someone checks it, it will be embarrassing. Our faith does not need exaggeration to hold it up.

The third witness is even more interesting. Pliny the Younger was governor of Bithynia, and in the early 110s AD he wrote to the emperor Trajan with a request for guidance: there are so many Christians, what should I do? He wrote that these people gather before dawn and sing hymns to Christ as to a god. You can tell this governor had a splitting headache. He did not care who Jesus was, but he left us a picture: ordinary people, up before daybreak, singing to a man who had been crucified.
Spiritual meaning: God is not afraid of being checked
Brothers and sisters, our Lord did not hide in a fog of legend. The Gospel of Luke pins the time Jesus began His ministry to a long list of names:

Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, (Luke 3:1-2)

Myths usually begin with “once upon a time, long, long ago.” Luke begins like an official document: the year, the titles, the territories, every one of them given. In 1961, archaeologists dug up a stone at Caesarea with Pilate’s name carved on it. The Bible is willing to be examined, because this God is willing to be met within history.
2. So what do the doubters say?
Some of you may ask: Pastor, is it really true that no scholar doubts Jesus’ existence? There are some, and we should state their case in full. That is basic respect.

They will say: Tacitus wrote more than eighty years after Jesus, and perhaps he was just listening to Christians; the Josephus passage has been altered; Paul’s letters say very little about Jesus’ earthly life; the Gospels were written by believers. The scholar Richard Carrier published an academic book in 2014 that uses probability methods to argue that Jesus began as a heavenly figure and was only later written as an earthly one.

These questions deserve to be taken seriously. And the academic world has taken them seriously. In 2017 the scholar Daniel Gullotta responded point by point in a professional journal and concluded that this hypothesis is hard to sustain.
An unbelieving scholar defends Jesus’ existence

The most interesting voice is the next one. The American New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman was a zealous evangelical in his youth, then left the faith, and describes himself as an agnostic. He has written several bestsellers that question Christianity. Yet in 2012 he wrote a book called Did Jesus Exist?, aimed squarely at refuting the claim that Jesus never existed.
One of his arguments is very simple: Paul says in his own words that he met Jesus’ brother.
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days. But of the other apostles I saw no one except James, the Lord’s brother. (Galatians 1:18-19)

My friends, it is very hard to have dinner with the younger brother of a mythical figure. When Paul wrote this letter, it was only about twenty years after the cross, and he had met James even earlier. Another argument is that the Jews of that time did not expect a crucified Messiah. The cross was shameful. Who would invent that as the opening scene of their own religion?

So here is where things stand today: on this point, believing and unbelieving historians mostly stand on the same side. Professor Dunn even said that Jesus’ baptism by John and His crucifixion under Pilate are historical facts that can hardly be doubted.
Spiritual meaning: do not fear questions, and do not exaggerate

Brothers and sisters, this section gives us two reminders. First, do not be afraid when friends ask questions. When someone asks, “Did Jesus really exist?”, he may be sincerely looking for the way. We should be glad, not nervous.

Second, do not exaggerate. There is a difficulty between the census Luke records and the date Josephus gives, and scholars have offered several solutions, none of them settled to this day. We can say frankly, “This point has not been resolved.” Honesty is itself a witness.
3. Knowing He existed is not enough
What Ehrman believes, and what you believe

At this point I need to pour a little cold water. Ehrman is one hundred percent sure that Jesus existed, yet he is not a Christian. Tacitus knew about Christ, and he did not believe. Pilate saw Jesus with his own eyes and questioned Him in person, and he did not believe either.

It is like knowing that TSMC’s headquarters is in Hsinchu: that does not make you its employee. You may know who the president is, and that does not mean you know him. Knowing that a person exists is the starting point of knowing him. It is not yet knowing him.
One event, two ways of writing it

Tacitus wrote Jesus’ death as a footnote: the head of a dangerous movement, executed by the authorities. Paul wrote about the very same cross, the very same historical event, and this is what he said:
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. (1 Corinthians 15:3)
Do you hear the difference? In Tacitus’ sentence, there are no words “for us.” History can tell you “He died.” Only the gospel tells you “for whom He died.”

This is the most moving part of the gospel: the One condemned by a Roman official went up willingly, so that the condemned could receive forgiveness. He did not only enter the first century AD. He wants to enter your year, that night of yours, that thing you cannot bring yourself to say.
Spiritual meaning: the faithfulness of the Word made flesh
But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman, born under the law. (Galatians 4:4)

God’s faithfulness is not an abstract concept. When the time of the promise came, He really came, into a world with tax collectors, governors and crying children. So we can rest assured that He will walk into your life just as really.

Brothers and sisters, what we have examined today is the most basic thing of all: this man existed. The records left by His enemies and the letters left by His friends all point to it. In the units ahead, we will keep asking: Are the books that record Him reliable? What did He say about Himself? Did He really rise from the dead?

In 321 we say that the Bible is our standard and Jesus is our example. A faith that can stand up to examination will turn our mindset from “Jesus is a story” into “Jesus is a Lord I must respond to.” When the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes. Let this real Jesus reign in your home and in your work.
Please be quiet for a moment. Picture that string of names in Luke 3:1, then add today’s date, and add your own name.

Lord Jesus, thank You that You did not leave behind only an idea but came in person to the human world and suffered under Pilate. Let me know the real You, and let my faith stand up to examination. If a friend wants to take You seriously for the first time today, reveal Yourself to him in person. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Are the Gospels Reliable? Grandma at the Reunion Table

Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. (John 20:30-31)

Brothers and sisters, peace! Suppose you are a traffic police officer. There has been an accident at an intersection, and four passersby stay behind to give statements. You look, and all four statements are exactly the same from the first word to the last, even down to the punctuation. Would you be deeply moved and say, “How reliable!”? No. You would ask: did you four get your story straight outside before coming in?

Now take a different case. All four say the red car ran the red light, but one says it was drizzling, another says the road was just damp; one stood on the east side and saw the driver’s face, another stood on the west side and only remembers the license plate. An experienced officer reading statements like these will actually sit up straight and read on carefully.

Today we are talking about the Gospels. Many friends have had this experience: you pick up the Bible and compare, and, hey, why does Matthew say it differently from Mark? Some people put the Bible down for good at that point. Today I am not going to put makeup on the Bible, and I will not tell you the problems are all solved. I want to show you what the scholars are actually arguing about, how far the argument goes, and where we can stand.
1. For those decades, how was the story passed on?

The estimate common in scholarship goes like this: Mark around AD 70, Matthew and Luke around AD 80 to 85, John around AD 90 to 95. This is the summary of Ehrman, a scholar who does not believe, and it is close to the mainstream. There are also Christian scholars, such as William Lane Craig, who argue for much earlier dates, with Luke perhaps in the AD 50s. We have to be honest: those who argue for early dates are a minority.

Whichever you adopt, between Jesus’ death and the first Gospel there lie several decades. Decades! Friends, I cannot even remember what we ate at last month’s fellowship lunch. So the skeptical friend has a fair question: over those decades, wouldn’t the story drift?
A game of telephone, or a reunion-dinner story?

Ehrman wrote a book called Jesus Before the Gospels. Using psychology and memory research, he tells us that human memory is very good at changing things, and group memory is the same: in the course of telling, stories get altered and even created. He holds that the Gospel authors were not eyewitnesses and had no access to eyewitnesses. This is the strongest argument on the other side, and we should respect it.

And on the other side? The Swedish scholar Birger Gerhardsson argued that the disciples passed on Jesus’ words somewhat the way Jewish rabbis taught their students, by memorizing. Later Kenneth Bailey, who lived for decades in the Middle East, proposed another picture: stories in a village are not recited word for word, but neither are they told any old way, because a whole community is watching over them.

This reminds me of the Lunar New Year’s Eve reunion dinner. Every year Uncle tells the story of how the whole family fled as refugees. This year there is an extra joke, next year a different adjective, and nobody minds. But if he gets the year of the escape wrong, or turns the person who saved the family into somebody else, Grandma puts down her chopsticks at once: “That’s not right!” The skeleton of the story has someone guarding it, and the details have room to breathe.

So the real question is this: is the story of Jesus more like a game of telephone, or more like a reunion-dinner story with Grandma sitting at the table? To be honest, Bailey’s examples come from modern Middle Eastern villages, and whether they can be carried straight back to the first century is still argued among scholars. But the opening lines of Luke at least tell us what he himself was trying to do.

Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed. (Luke 1:1-4)
Spiritual meaning: faith has always been entrusted into human hands

Brothers and sisters, from the very beginning the gospel has been one person telling another. God chose this road, which carries risk and is also very humble. The faith you hold today is the same: someone once sat next to you and told it to you. You too are a person at that reunion table, and you are to guard the skeleton, neither adding carelessly nor cutting carelessly.
2. A gentlemanly contest between two scholars
Bauckham says: the witnesses were still alive

In 2006 the British scholar Richard Bauckham published Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, and in 2017 a revised edition appeared. He argues that the Synoptic Gospels stay quite close to the testimony of eyewitnesses, and that the Gospel of John comes from an eyewitness whom he identifies as John the Elder. Notice that his view is not quite the same as the apostle John we usually hear about in Sunday school. That is how scholars are: even those on the same side do not all agree.

One of his arguments is rather fun: personal names. An Israeli scholar, Tal Ilan, collected the names of Palestinian Jews of that period into a database. Bauckham checked the Gospels against it and found that the distribution of names matches very well. Names like Simon and Joseph were everywhere then, just as in a Taiwanese classroom today you might find three students named Jiahao. So the Gospels have to clarify: which Simon? Simon Peter, or Simon of Cyrene?

Mark even writes that this Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross, was “the father of Alexander and Rufus.” Why mention the sons’ names? Bauckham thinks it may be because the readers knew the two brothers: if you don’t believe it, go and ask them.
Ehrman says: no. And others kept the argument going

In 2016 Ehrman and Bauckham held a public conversation on a British radio program. Ehrman praised the other man as a fine scholar and also said plainly that they disagree on many questions. Those of us who share the gospel must never say “all scholars agree.” Ehrman is not our supporter. He is a serious opponent, and when we cite him we must be faithful to his position.

In 2023 Gregor and Blais published a statistical study arguing that this phenomenon of names can be explained just as well by transmission in anonymous communities. Then van de Weghe and Wilson responded that the other side’s testing method was flawed, and that the distribution of names in the Gospels fits better with historical sources than with fiction or modern historical novels. The battle is still being fought. My advice: if you find it interesting, you can mention it, but do not treat it as your trump card.

Let me give one more example. In the early second century the church leader Papias said that Mark wrote down Peter’s teaching from memory. This is a very early clue, but Ehrman considers Papias almost entirely unreliable, while other scholars think he deserves serious attention. When a clue is disputed, we tell people honestly that it is disputed.
Spiritual meaning: you do not have to win every round in order to believe

Many Christians are afraid of this kind of discussion, as if one unanswerable question would bring the whole faith down. But faith is like an old bridge held up by many beams together. That one of them is under repair does not mean you cannot cross the bridge today. First Peter says to always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, “with humility and fear.” Humility, precisely because we know there are things we ourselves do not know.
3. Differences and embarrassments: what the authors forgot to hide
The synagogue leader’s daughter: was she dead or not?

Mark records the synagogue leader Jairus saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death.” Matthew records, “My daughter has just died.” That is quite a difference! The centurion’s story is the same: Matthew says the centurion came forward himself to ask Jesus, while Luke says he sent several elders and friends.

What do we do? The scholar Michael Licona compared Plutarch’s biographies, where the same event is written up in different people’s lives with compression, displacement and spotlighting. He argues that the Gospel authors used similar techniques. It is like telling your wife, “I called the bank today,” when in fact your secretary placed the call; nobody would say you were lying. The evangelical scholar Mark Strauss praised the book and also admitted that some will feel Licona goes too far, because it touches on how we understand inerrancy. And many brothers and sisters prefer to read in the traditional harmonizing way. All of this is discussion within reverence for Scripture, and we do not need to condemn one another.
If they were making it up, why not make it up better?

There is another kind of material worth a closer look. Scholars have a tool called the criterion of embarrassment: the church would hardly fabricate material that is unflattering to itself. Mark records that in His hometown Jesus “could do no mighty work.” Jesus Himself says that of that day, “nor the Son” knows. And the first leader of the church denied his Lord three times. None of this helps the publicity at all.

Of course this tool has limits, and some scholars remind us that it cannot settle historicity by itself. But at least it shows us that the material in these authors’ hands has edges and corners, and they did not sand it all smooth.
“But of that day or that hour no one knows—not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. (Mark 13:32)
Spiritual meaning: reliability is for the sake of life

The Gospel of John itself says that Jesus did many things that were not written down. The author selected, and he had a purpose. He did not pretend to be a neutral surveillance camera, and he says plainly: these things were written that you may believe and have life. At this point someone will say: isn’t that just bias? Friends, a survivor of a concentration camp also writes a memoir with a purpose, hoping you will not forget. A witness with a purpose is not an unreliable witness. You just have to check.

So, back to the intersection. How far can historical study walk? It can say: these documents are quite early in date, their form is ancient biography, and they contain much material that is unfavorable to their authors; how close they stand to the eyewitnesses is still debated by scholars. What it cannot do is take that final step for you and say, “This Jesus is the Son of God, who died for my sins and rose again.” That step is called faith. But faith does not have to be taken with eyes closed.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 framework says: the Bible is my standard. A standard is to be used, not set up on a shelf. Many people have heard countless sermons in a lifetime and never read a single Gospel from beginning to end. This week, please read Mark in one sitting. It takes about two hours, shorter than a movie. As you read, mark the places that puzzle you and take them to your spiritual companion.

This is also a practice of moving from self-centered to selfless. The self-centered way of reading puts me on the judge’s seat, picking faults in the Bible, or picking only what I like to hear. The selfless way of reading may also ask questions and wrestle, but in the end is willing to let the passage question me: will you let Jesus reign?

To the friends who have not yet come to faith, I am not asking you to believe every word of the Bible today. I only invite you to read it yourself once, and not just hear it secondhand, whether from me or from Ehrman.

Faithful Lord, thank You that I can come to know You through these testimonies. When I have questions, I will bring them honestly before You; what I do not understand, give me patience. May I read not only words but meet the Jesus who died and rose for me. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Who Did He Say He Was? The Convenience Store Clerk and Your Mortgage
Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.” (John 8:58)

Brothers and sisters, peace! Imagine you are coming home from work in the evening and stop at the convenience store at the mouth of the alley to buy a bottle of soy milk. When you check out, the clerk scans the barcode, looks up, and says very gently, “Sir, that mortgage of yours? I’ve canceled it for you.”

How would you react? I guess you would slowly pick up your soy milk and slowly back away. Either this person is under too much stress, or he has just bought the whole bank. There are not many other possibilities.

Two thousand years ago, in Capernaum, in a house whose roof had been torn open, something just like this happened. Four friends lowered a paralyzed man through the roof, and everyone waited to see a miracle. Jesus looked at the man and said something else entirely.

Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” But there were some of the scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:5-7)

Notice that the logic of those scribes was actually very clear. They understood the weight of that sentence better than many modern people. Today we ask: how did Jesus actually see Himself? We will walk this line in layers, because part of it is what the text says, part of it is what historians argue about, and part of it you have to answer for yourself.
1. Three declarations that make you shift in your seat
Son of Man: it sounds ordinary and is not

The title Jesus loved best to use for Himself in the Gospels is “Son of Man.” In Aramaic this phrase can mean simply “a person,” a bit like our saying “your humble servant.” Quite modest, isn’t it? But open Daniel chapter 7 and there is a startling picture.

I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him near before him. Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. (Daniel 7:13-14)

Mark records that on the night of His trial, the high priest asked Jesus whether He was the Christ, and He answered, “I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.” The high priest tore his clothes. The most humble-sounding title hid the least humble declaration.

Let us go back to the paralyzed man. If I wrong you, you may forgive me, and that makes sense. But if a third party walks up and says, “What he owes you, I’ll write off,” you will surely ask: who do you think you are? Jesus was forgiving the debts the man had owed, all his life, to God and to people. C. S. Lewis pointed out the same thing: such words make sense only when the speaker is the very Lord who has been offended.

And then there is the Sabbath. Jesus said, “the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” Who established the Sabbath? It is written in the Ten Commandments: God did. To use an analogy, if someone walked into a courthouse and said, “The constitution was made for the people, so I am the master of the constitution,” those listening would hardly take it as a joke.
Before Abraham came into existence, I AM

The third declaration is the most direct. In John chapter 8, Jesus argues with His opponents in the temple. They say: “You are not yet fifty years old! Have you seen Abraham?” Jesus answers, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.” Listen to the grammar. If He only meant that He was old, He would have said, “I existed before Abraham.” He does not say “I was.” He says “I AM,” in Greek ego eimi.
A Jewish listener’s ears would immediately think of that scene at the burning bush.
God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” (Exodus 3:14)

Did the people of that day understand? The next verse says they took up stones to throw at Him. By chapter 10 they state their reason more plainly: “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God.”

Let me add one more thing here. The way John writes is very different from the first three Gospels. Many historians think these sayings are an expression of later, deepened theology, while Christians believe they faithfully convey who Jesus was. So when you talk with an unbelieving friend, starting from the forgiveness of sins in Mark will put you on firmer ground than starting from John 8:58.
Spiritual meaning: He will not let you leave Him on the shelf

Many people like to place Jesus next to Confucius and Socrates, a row of great masters, handy for reference. These passages make that arrangement very uncomfortable. The masters say, “The Way is over there.” Jesus often says, “Come to me.” Brothers and sisters, our everyday faith can make the same mistake: we treat Him as a consultant, called in when there is trouble. But a Lord who can say “your sins are forgiven” cannot be only a consultant.
2. The historians’ dispute: we must speak honestly

At this point someone will raise a hand: Pastor, everything you have quoted is from the Gospels. Did the historical Jesus really talk like this? That is a very good question. The unbelieving scholar Bart Ehrman, in his 2014 book How Jesus Became God, argues that the historical Jesus did not call Himself God. Sayings like “I and the Father are one,” he thinks, are a later development. He even thinks the Son of Man in Jesus’ mouth refers to another figure yet to come.

But Ehrman also says something important: soon after Jesus’ death, the disciples believed He had been exalted to divine status. Note that he is not a Christian, and he takes care to say that he writes as a historian. We must not describe him as a supporter, but even he admits this: the timing was very early.

Another scholar, Larry Hurtado, spent his life studying how the earliest Christians worshiped. He wrote Lord Jesus Christ, over seven hundred pages, and his argument is simple and startling: devotion to Jesus appeared astonishingly early, and those doing it were Jews who held strictly to one God. Friends, Jews were willing to shed blood to avoid idolatry, and yet they offered worship to a man who had been crucified not long before, and felt they were not betraying the one God! That needs explaining.

Richard Bauckham goes further and points out that the New Testament writers include Jesus within the identity of the one God of Israel. His example is Philippians chapter 2. Paul draws on exactly God’s oath in Isaiah: “to me every knee shall bow.” Yet what Paul writes is “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.” This letter is generally thought to have been written between the AD 50s and the early 60s, only two or three decades after the crucifixion.

There is also an interesting scholar, Daniel Boyarin, a Jewish scholar who is not a Christian. He argues that the expectation of the Son of Man as a divine figure was already there inside Judaism at the time. Other scholars think he goes too far, and Ehrman holds that the Son of Man in Daniel is a symbol of Israel. So there is no settled answer here, and we say so as it is.
Lunatic, Liar or Lord: useful, but do not use it alone

Many brothers and sisters like to use Lewis’ argument when sharing the gospel: a man who says things like this cannot be merely a good teacher; he is either a lunatic, or the Devil, or God. In Mere Christianity this passage is powerful, and it reminds us that “good teacher” is not a position that stands firm.

But I must remind you that it has a premise: that Jesus really said these things. Critics say the fourth possibility is legend, and even the Christian philosopher William Lane Craig admits that the argument is incomplete. So please do not use it as a three-second winning weapon. Combine it with the Gospel sources we discussed in the last unit, and talk it through slowly. Honesty is itself a witness.
Spiritual meaning: a Lord who does not fear examination

That Christian faith has these debates shows that it places itself inside history. We need not panic because scholars disagree, nor reduce the disagreement to “they all agree with me.” We can take time to investigate and take time to answer.
3. Going to the cross with this kind of authority

If a man had this kind of authority, how do you suppose he would use it? There have been plenty in history who considered themselves gods, and they usually built palaces, collected taxes and put up statues. And this One?

who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:6-8)

We often assume that having authority means clinging to it. This One went the other way, down. Back to the convenience store: this is not a clerk talking nonsense. It is the owner of the bank taking off his suit, standing behind the counter, and emptying his own account to pay off your mortgage. “Your sins are forgiven” is not a cheap sentence; it was paid for in the end with a cross.
Spiritual meaning: letting Jesus reign begins with bending the knee

The 321 framework has a line: letting God be God and people be people. The self-centered person always wants to stand on the other side of the counter, as judge of his own life and judge of others. The selfless person knows that the authority to forgive is in His hands, and my place is on my knees. And the Lord before whom we kneel first knelt for me. Brothers and sisters, is there a room in your life that still has a sign on the door: “No entry, Jesus included”? Money, marriage, temper, or that person you will not forgive?

This is as far as we walk today. What the text says is clear. How scholars argue has also been said. History cannot answer the last question for you. To the friends who have not yet come to faith, I ask only that you not file Him too quickly under good teacher, because that is the one label He Himself left us no room for. Go and read Mark chapter 2, and then ask Him: Who are You?

To the brothers and sisters who already believe, this week please write down one sentence: if Jesus is Lord, the one thing I will change this week is what? Then tell your spiritual companion. Bending the knee is not a slogan. It has to land in that phone call on Wednesday afternoon, that bill, that sentence. When He reigns in the smallest corners of our lives, others can see who He is.

Lord Jesus, I confess that I often only want to use You and am unwilling to obey You. You are worthy of every knee bowing, yet for me You took the form of a servant and went to the cross. Reign in my life, forgive my sins, and let my tongue sincerely confess that You are Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. How did the convenience store clerk illustration help you understand the words “your sins are forgiven”? How did you understand this passage before?
2. When a friend says “Jesus was just a good teacher,” how would you answer so as to honestly acknowledge the scholarly debate without giving up your witness?
3. In which area of your life is Jesus still only an advisor and not Lord? What concrete step can you take this week?
Miracles: The Hand Over the Billiard Table

Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. (Matthew 11:4-5)

Brothers and sisters, peace! When you get home tonight, please put two thousand-dollar bills into a drawer. Tomorrow you open it and find only one. What do you do? You will probably ask the children at home, or check the door lock. I am sure nobody will phone the mathematics department and say: Professor, disaster, one plus one no longer equals two!

This little drawer is today’s theme. Many people feel that believing in miracles means not believing in science. We have friends who are scientists here today, and I am a little nervous. But I would like us to ask together: if a miracle happens, what is it that gets broken?

Let me make clear two things I will not do today. First, I will not tell you that science has proved miracles. There is no such thing. Second, if there is someone here who has been sick for years and has prayed a long time without being healed, I will not hand you a neat formula. We will come back to you in a moment.
A short essay that changed the West

Let us go back to Britain in 1748. The Scottish philosopher David Hume published an essay called “Of Miracles.” His definition is famous: a miracle is a violation of the laws of nature. His reasoning is also powerful: where do the laws of nature come from? They are built up from the uniform experience of all humankind. Dead people have never come back to life, and that experience is as strong as experience can be. So if someone tells you he saw a dead man rise, which is more probable, that he is mistaken or lying, or that a dead man rose?

Friends, this question is powerful, and I hope you will respect it. Hume also said that those who speak of miracles are often carrying passion and self-interest, and that every religion has its miracle stories, which cancel one another out. Brothers and sisters, that is hard to hear, but is it not true? Those people on television who lay on hands and ask you to give an offering first have done Hume the best publicity in the world.
Light through the crack in the door

Two hundred and fifty years later, in the year 2000, the philosopher of science John Earman wrote a book with a very blunt title, Hume’s Abject Failure. Step by step with probability theory, he showed that Hume’s reasoning does not hold: enough independent testimonies can, in principle, overcome a very low probability. Notice that Earman’s book criticizes Hume’s logic; he is not preaching the gospel for Christianity. And some scholars of Hume have replied that he reads Hume too narrowly. So this battle is not over.

Now look at Lewis. In his 1947 book Miracles he used the drawer example: the laws of mathematics did not break; something else happened. Let me offer a picture too. On a billiard table, the laws of physics can work out the path of the cue ball after it hits the red one. But if you reach in halfway and pick up the red ball, are the laws broken? No. Momentum is still calculated, gravity is still calculated; there is simply one more hand. The laws tell you what happens “when nobody touches it”; they do not guarantee that there is no hand.
Spiritual meaning: the real question is upstream

At this point, our atheist friends will say, quite fairly: wait, you must first prove that there is a hand. Yes! So the question upstream of miracles is the question of God. If the universe is simply a billiard table in a closed room, of course there will be no hand. If this table has always had a Maker who owns it, then His reaching in violates nothing. We admit honestly that this is an inference from worldview and not a laboratory result.

Next I want to talk about a study the church does not much like to mention. In 2006 a large American study called STEP randomly divided 1,802 patients having heart bypass surgery into groups. Some were prayed for and some were not. The result? There was no significant difference in complications. More awkward still, the patients who knew for certain that people were praying for them had slightly more complications, 59 percent versus 51 percent. Later the Cochrane review also said that most studies could see no effect, though overall the evidence is inconclusive.

There is another side. In 2010 Brown and colleagues went to Mozambique to study face-to-face prayer with the laying on of hands, and the hearing and vision measurements of 24 subjects improved. But there was no control group and the number was small, so the effect of expectation cannot be ruled out. Professor Keener wrote two large volumes called Miracles, over a thousand pages, collecting testimonies from around the world, and he himself says that these are evidence and not proof, and that not every one is supernatural.

So what should we say? Here is what I say: prayer is not a pill you can put through a double-blind trial. God is personal; He is not a vending machine, and He will not fit Himself into our research plans. But I also have to remind myself that this sentence cannot become an all-purpose excuse. We cannot call it a miracle when it works and a mystery when it fails, and then pretend that is fair. Both sides must be honest.

Can history speak of miracles? Ehrman says no: history can only say “what probably happened,” and a miracle by definition is the least probable, so a historian cannot draw that conclusion. He stresses that he is not claiming miracles can never exist. Licona replies that to call it the least probable, you must first assume that God is unlikely to intervene, and that is also a worldview. My own view is that this conversation lets us see clearly where each side begins, and so we can have a little less heat between us.
Spiritual meaning: do not sell miracles

Brothers and sisters, I am saying all this so plainly today because we must guard the name of God. To treat miracles as merchandise, to make people give an offering before they can be healed, or to tell a sick person, “Your faith is not enough,” is not the gospel. If you are under that kind of pressure, please walk away from it. Asking God for healing and seeing a doctor do not conflict; medicine and doctors are both gifts of God, and if you have persistent symptoms, please go and see one.

So the next time someone shares a miracle testimony with you, how can you listen? I suggest three questions, not to throw cold water but to protect the thing. First, what happened? Are there medical records, and what did the doctor say before and after? Professor Keener himself admits that not every case is supernatural, and that some may be natural causes or even fraud, so looking at each case on its own is reasonable. Second, to whom does the glory go? To Jesus, or to some speaker and his next conference? Third, where does the money go? In the book of Acts a man named Simon wanted to buy this kind of power with money, and Peter answered him, “May your silver perish with you.” That road was closed two thousand years ago.
A road sign is not the destination

The Gospel of John almost never uses the word “wonder”; it mostly calls them “signs.” Friends, when you are driving on the expressway and see a sign that says “Taipei, 30 kilometers,” you do not stop the car, hug the sign and take a photo, saying: I have arrived! The job of a sign is to make you look up.
This beginning of his signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him. (John 2:11)

Jesus saw it that way Himself. After the five thousand were fed, the crowd chased after Him, and He said, “you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.” In plain words: what you want is lunch boxes, not me. Today we also have to ask ourselves: do I want what is in His hand, or do I want Him?

If you read the Gospels carefully, you will find that Jesus did many miracles and also refused several times. The devil told Him to turn stones into bread, and He would not. King Herod waited a long time and “hoped to see some miracle done by him,” but Jesus “gave no answers.” When people came asking for a sign, He said, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign.” If He had wanted to be famous, these were all golden chances. His miracles were never a performance. Most were because someone was standing there in need, or because He wanted to bring people to Himself. At the end of his book John states his purpose very clearly.

Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. (John 20:30-31)
Notice his candor: there were many more that were not written down, and he did not plan to hold a press conference for each one. What he wants you to have is not a list of miracles but life.

Now I want to go back to what I promised at the start of today. John the Baptist, in prison, sent people to ask Jesus: Are You the one? Jesus replied: the blind see, the lame walk. But notice that when John heard this, he was still in prison, and in the end he was not rescued. Paul asked three times, and the thorn stayed.
He has said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

Dear friend, if you have prayed for many years and have not received, I will not tell you that this must be God’s good will. I do not know why. I only know that Jesus does not ask you to pretend you are not hurting. He Himself on the cross cried out “why.” And that day He did not come down from the cross. He could have, while people below mocked Him, “save yourself!” He stayed there for our sins. On the third day He rose from the dead, and that is the greatest sign, and the pledge to all who are still waiting.
Spiritual meaning: letting God be God

So the 321 framework says: letting God be God and people be people. We may ask boldly, and we must be willing to keep company. We cannot write checks on God’s behalf, and we cannot decide for Him whose faith is not enough. From the human, temporary viewpoint, the biggest question is whether it turned out well this time. From God’s eternal viewpoint, even in the greatest miracle, Lazarus died again later. What we wait for is the day with no tears.

This week, please do one thing: visit or check in on someone who has been ill for a long time. Do not offer advice, and do not share who ate what and got better. Just ask one question: how can I pray for you? And then really pray. People matter more than tasks, and he is not a display piece for your faith.

To the friends who have not yet come to faith, I do not ask you to believe today because of one testimony. I ask you to think: if there really were a Maker who owns this table, would you let His hand come into your life?

Lord Jesus, You could calm the wind and the sea, and on the cross You also went through the night of not being rescued. I bring my sickness and my waiting to You, and I ask You to heal; my faith is small, so help me. Give me grace that is sufficient, and strengthen my hope of the resurrection. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Have you ever seen or experienced something you regard as a miracle? Using the layers learned today, how would you describe which parts are fact and which are your faith interpretation?
2. How did the result of the STEP study make you feel? How would you answer a friend who brought this study to you?
3. When facing someone who has long gone unhealed, what are we most likely to say wrongly? How can you concretely keep company with such a person this week?
The Sermon on the Mount: Teaching That Turns the World Upside Down
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. (Matthew 5:3)

Brothers and sisters, peace! Suppose a company is hiring today, and the job ad reads: “Wanted: the poor in spirit, people who often mourn, the gentle, those who are very hungry, those who are persecuted.” Would you think this company is about to collapse?
But two thousand years ago, Jesus went up on the mountain, sat down, and began to read out exactly this list, and said: blessed are these people!

Stranger still, this teaching, which takes only a dozen minutes or so to read from start to finish, went on to enter the hearts of some people you would never expect. A young Hindu lawyer read it and said it went straight to his heart. An African American pastor, in the days when his house was bombed, walked back to this passage. A German pastor wrote a book on it in the Nazi era, and later died on the gallows.
Today we walk into Jesus Hall to see why this teaching turned the world upside down, and also why in the end it brings us to grace.
1. The list of blessings that lays the ladder down

The list of blessings in our generation is familiar to everyone: how much your annual salary is, how many square feet your home has, which school your child attends. Life is like climbing a ladder, and the higher you climb, the more blessed you are.

Jesus’ list lays the ladder down and turns it into a bridge. The first to walk onto the bridge are those who can no longer climb. To be poor in spirit is to know in your heart that your hands are empty; to mourn is to stop pretending that everything is fine.

The Greek word for “blessed” is makarios, and one English word can hardly capture it. The New Testament scholar Jonathan Pennington argues that the Beatitudes portray what real flourishing looks like for people centered on God. Friends, this is not a loyalty card where you collect eight stamps and claim a prize. It is a painting, and what it paints is the face of the citizens of the kingdom.
Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. (Matthew 5:5-6)
From the hands into the heart

Then Jesus did something that makes people even more uncomfortable. Six times He said, “You have heard that it was said… but I tell you.” Do not murder? Yes, but what about the fire in your heart? Do not commit adultery? Yes, but what about your eyes?

It is as if you show your medical checkup report to the doctor, every figure is in the normal range apart from a few marked in red, and you feel rather pleased. The doctor says: “I have looked at the numbers. Let’s talk about your heart.”

In chapter six He asks again: when you give to the needy, for whom are you doing it? When you pray, for whose ears? Someone checks in on Facebook to announce that they are fasting. Brothers and sisters, a reward like that is paid in full the moment the likes come in.
Spiritual meaning: the law of the kingdom reaches the inner room

So the Sermon on the Mount is not a loftier list of moral rules. It shines God’s light into the inner room where we shut the door. We can fool our coworkers and fool our spouses, but we cannot fool the Father who sees in secret. That is frightening, and it also sets us free, because we no longer have to perform.
2. Three people and the hardest sentence
The hardest sentence of Jesus is probably this one:

But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. (Matthew 5:44-45)

Let us look at three real people. Gandhi wrote in his autobiography that the New Testament made a very different impression on him, especially the Sermon on the Mount, which went straight to his heart, and he compared it with the Bhagavad Gita. But note that Gandhi never became a Christian, and we should not describe him as one.

By the way, there is a saying online attributed to Gandhi: “I like your Christ, I do not like your Christians.” It spreads easily, but we cannot find a reliable first-hand source for it. We do not share the gospel with sayings of unknown origin, because one falsehood can damage the whole witness.

Pastor King, recalling the Montgomery bus boycott, said that Christ furnished the spirit and the motivation and Gandhi furnished the method. He was a pastor who believed in Jesus, and at the height of hatred he chose not to answer hatred with hatred.

In 1937 Bonhoeffer published Discipleship, which centers on an exposition of the Sermon on the Mount, and he warned the church not to turn grace into cheap grace. Later he was arrested for his involvement in the plot against Hitler, and on April 9, 1945, he died at Flossenbürg. Friends, how to evaluate his involvement in that plot is still discussed among Christians today. He was not a man who made hard questions sound simple.

Some friends will ask: aren’t these words found elsewhere too? Yes. Confucius said not to do to others what you do not want done to yourself; the Jewish rabbi Hillel has a similar saying. Russell also noted that Lao Tzu and the Buddha taught similar principles. Christians need not be anxious or deny it. Rays of goodness have always been scattered among people.

What is truly unusual is where the speaker places Himself. He does not say, “The ancient books say so.” He says, “But I tell you.” He also says that whether a man’s house stands or falls depends on how he treats “these words of mine.” That is why the crowds were astonished.

Another question is sharper. The philosopher Nietzsche thought that virtues such as gentleness and not taking revenge are really the weak calling their inability to win a fight morality. Friends, we need to take this criticism in, because some people really do use forgiveness as a cover for their fear.

But when Jesus spoke of gentleness, He held the choice in His hands. King and Bonhoeffer also took this road only after seeing the cost clearly. Whether gentleness is weakness or strength, history can offer only witnesses; in the end it depends on what you believe.
Spiritual meaning: this is not telling victims to be silent

I want to stop here and say something special. “Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.” This sentence addresses the heart of revenge. It does not ask anyone to remain in violence. When Jesus Himself was slapped by an officer, He spoke up and asked him, “why do you beat me?”

So if you or someone you know is suffering domestic violence or abuse, seeking safety and professional help is right, and the church should walk with you. Anyone who uses this verse to send you back to be beaten is misusing the Bible.
3. The highest standard leads us to the deepest grace
An exam paper no one passes
If, as we get here, you begin to feel uncomfortable inside, congratulations: you have understood. Jesus ends this section by saying:
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect. (Matthew 5:48)

Perfect? Like the Father? If this were the exam for getting into heaven, no one sitting here today would pass, and neither would the person at this pulpit. Many people think the Sermon on the Mount means “be a good person and you can go to heaven,” but it actually shuts that road.

This exam paper works like a mirror. A mirror will not wash your face; it only lets you see that your face is dirty. That is why the first sentence matters so much: the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor in spirit, to those who know their hands are empty.
The Lord who walked this road Himself

And the One who wrote this exam paper sat it Himself and scored full marks. He taught us to pray for those who persecute us, and when He was nailed to the cross He said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.”

Paul goes a step further: “while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.” Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? Loving enemies is not only what God asks of us; it is exactly how God treats us. We are the enemy.

for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. (Ephesians 2:8-10)
Spiritual meaning: grace first, obedience after

Notice the order: salvation is by grace, and only then comes “for good works.” We are not loved after we do well; we are loved, and then we begin to learn. It is like a child learning to walk: a father does not wait until the child walks steadily before claiming him. Because the child is already his son, he lifts him up again and again.

We often say that the self-centered person puts himself at the center, and the selfless person lets Jesus reign. Being poor in spirit is the first step of selflessness. No longer in a hurry to prove ourselves, no longer counting who saw, we can leave the credit with God, because “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
The Bible is my standard, and people matter more than tasks

The Sermon on the Mount is not a motto on the wall; it is our standard. We do not need to do it all at once. Choose one verse each week to live out. Jesus also said that before bringing your gift, if you remember that your brother has something against you, go first and be reconciled. So in His eyes, relationships come before ministry: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

This week’s action is simple: write down the name of one person who troubles you, and for seven days in a row pray one sentence for them, asking only that God would bless them. If this person has deeply hurt you, you may first hand the pain over to God, and you need not force more. Changing your mindset, changing your life, changing your daily living often begins with a short prayer like this.

Brothers and sisters, the Sermon on the Mount ends with two houses. Rain falls, floods come, winds blow; one house stands and one falls. On the outside they may look exactly alike, and the difference is underground. Where will you and I build our lives? He is not telling us to work hard at being a better self. He invites us to set our foundation on Him.

Let us be quiet for a moment and think of that person who makes our chest tighten at the memory. Let us pray: Father in heaven, I confess that I cannot live out this teaching on my own. Forgive my pride and my anger, give me a poor spirit, and give me grace to pray for the one who hurt me. If I am in danger now, lead me to safety and help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Which of the Beatitudes makes you most uncomfortable? Which comforts you most? Why?
2. How do you respond to Nietzsche’s criticism that gentleness is only the self-consolation of the weak? Have you ever seen gentleness that had real strength?
3. How do you tell the difference between forgiving and letting violence continue? How can the church walk with those who have been hurt?
A Flawless Character: Who Dares Ask This Question?
Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? (John 8:46)

Brothers and sisters, peace! Let me start by giving you homework, and don’t be afraid. Tonight when you get home, ask your wife, your husband or your roommate one question: “Can you point out what is wrong with me?” But first brew a pot of tea and pull up a chair, because the answer will be long. Some couples have tried it and still haven’t finished.

Someone in the Gospels asked this very question. Not at a cozy small group meeting, but to a crowd of opponents who were looking for something to seize on. Jesus said, “Which of you convicts me of sin?” Friends, if anyone here dares to ask this at their own company’s year-end banquet, I will admire them, and I will also be worried.

This sentence has only two possibilities. Either this man is arrogant beyond help, or this man’s life really is different. Today we will not hurry to a conclusion. We will do three things: first see how He treated people, then invite the harshest critics onto the stage, and finally ask whom such a character is living for.

If you read the four Gospels as one appointment calendar, you will notice something interesting: this man’s schedule keeps getting interrupted. He is hurrying along, and children are brought to Him; He is passing through a town, and a tax collector is up a tree; He is eating at someone’s house, and a woman comes in weeping. If He had a personal assistant, that assistant would probably have a stomach ulcer by now.

Let us look at one scene. The law of Moses required a person with leprosy to cover his upper lip and cry, “Unclean! Unclean!” and to live alone outside the camp. Think about it: wherever he goes, he has to broadcast on his own behalf, “Everybody keep away, I’m not clean.” After a few years of that, even he himself believes it.

A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, “If you want to, you can make me clean.” Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.” (Mark 1:40-41)

Some scholars remind us that the “leprosy” in the Gospels mostly refers broadly to skin diseases, not necessarily Hansen’s disease as we speak of it today, and that the heart of the problem was ritual uncleanness. That makes the picture clearer, if anything. He could have healed with a word, and He did that in other places. But this time He reached out first. That man may not have been touched by anyone in many years. A white shirt that touches a stain gets stained; bleach that touches a stain makes the stain retreat. Everyone feared catching it from him, but when Jesus touched him, the contagion ran the other way.

At this point, the Jesus in some people’s minds starts turning into a man who is always smiling, with flowing hair and a soft voice, like a shampoo commercial. Please put that picture down. Mark records that in the synagogue there was a man with a withered hand, and a group of people were watching Jesus to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath, so they could accuse Him.

When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored as healthy as the other. (Mark 3:5)

Anger, and grief at the same time. It is rare to see those two words together. When we get angry, it is mostly because someone stepped on our face, our parking space, our standing in the family chat group. And His anger? When the disciples kept the children away, He was moved with indignation; when people would rather keep the rules than see a hand restored, He looked around with anger. His anger was almost always aimed at those who keep people out.

A word in passing. When we speak of how Jesus treated women and the excluded, we often carelessly paint the Judaism of that time as unrelieved darkness to set Jesus off. The Jewish New Testament scholar Professor Amy-Jill Levine reminds Christians that this is a stereotype. Jesus Himself was a Jew, and His compassion has roots in the Jewish tradition. To praise Jesus, we need not first trample on His own people.
Spiritual meaning: goodness has a direction

Brothers and sisters, we often understand a “good person” to be someone who does not cause trouble and does not offend anyone. Jesus’ goodness is not of that kind. His goodness has a direction: it keeps flowing toward the forgotten. So when 321 says that people matter more than tasks and relationships matter more than things, this is not a management slogan. It is copied from Jesus’ appointment calendar.
2. Let the critic take the stage

Now I want to invite a very weighty person onto the stage. On March 6, 1927, the English philosopher Bertrand Russell gave his famous lecture “Why I Am Not a Christian” at Battersea Town Hall in London. He was gracious: he first affirmed Jesus’ teachings such as turning the other cheek, and took the chance to jibe that Christians do not manage it. That cut we have to accept.

Then he made three points. First, he said a truly compassionate person would not believe in eternal punishment, and hell is a cruel doctrine. Second, when Jesus sent the demons into the pigs, it was really unfair to the pigs. Third, Jesus cursed the fig tree, yet Mark himself says it was not the season for figs, so what had the tree done wrong? His conclusion was that for wisdom and for virtue, he would put the Buddha and Socrates ahead of Jesus.

Friends, if you are hearing this for the first time today, you may be squirming a little. No need to be nervous. If someone’s faith is afraid of hearing these words, that faith needed strengthening in any case.

The fig tree: most interpreters read it as a prophetic sign-act. If you open the Gospel of Mark you will find it is sandwiched around the cleansing of the temple: tree, temple, tree. The point is aimed at a religion that is full of leaves and cannot bear fruit. This reading has a basis in the text. But if you read it and still feel something is off, I will not tell you to swallow that feeling. Just take it with you and keep asking.

There is a harder passage still, harder than any Russell picked. A Gentile mother came to ask Jesus to save her daughter, and Jesus actually said, “it is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Some scholars say plainly that this is an insult. In 2024 a scholar, Croy, argued in New Testament Studies that the diminutive in the original is closer to “little dogs” and that the point is the order of Jewish priority. The argument is not over. What we can be sure of is that the mother answered back beautifully, that Jesus gave way on the spot to her words, and that the Gospel honestly records the scene without retouching Him.

Hell is the heaviest, and Russell asked the right question. Let me say first that the church has often used hell to frighten people, and we should repent of that history. Within evangelicalism there are also different understandings of the nature of hell: the traditional view is eternal punishment; some scholars argue that the end is destruction, and Pastor John Stott in Britain cautiously raised this view in 1988. We will not rule between them here. But there is one thing all agree on: when Jesus spoke of judgment, He was not standing on high watching the show. When He saw Jerusalem, He wept over it. And in a world with no judgment at all, to whom would those who were oppressed all their lives bring their tears? That question is just as real. We put the difficulties on both sides on the table.
Spiritual meaning: even historians remember those three years

In the nineteenth century there was an Irish historian, Lecky, who was quite critical of church history in his History of European Morals. Yet when he wrote about Jesus, he said that the simple record of three short years of active life has done more to regenerate and soften mankind than all the writings of philosophers and the exhortations of moralists. Note that this is an assessment of influence; he was not endorsing “Jesus was sinless.” Neither should we speak for him beyond that.

To be honest, historians cannot verify whether a person has sinned. The sources were written by people who loved Him, and no source can open a person’s heart. So “Jesus was sinless” is not an archaeological discovery. It is a declaration of faith. Then what can we check? We can ask: does this declaration fit the record He left? Do the people who say it have standing to say it?

Look at who says it. Peter! This man followed Him for years, ate with Him, hurried along the road with Him, saw Him tired and saw Him weep. And he himself denied Him in front of a servant girl. This letter is traditionally attributed to Peter, and the question of authorship is also discussed among scholars, but the early church remembered him this way. Friends, when you have lived alongside a person for three years and still are willing to say he did not sin, that is worth more than any letter of recommendation.

who didn’t sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.” When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously. (1 Peter 2:22-23)

But I must remind everyone: if the story stopped here, it would be bad news for us. A perfect man standing in front of you is only a ruler to measure you by, and after measuring, you are only more despairing. Some children who meet a piano teacher who plays too well end up not wanting to touch the piano at all, and that is the same principle.
The good news of the New Testament is in the next step. This flawless One did not stay on high giving us grades. He walked to the place where we should stand.
For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. (2 Corinthians 5:21)

Notice the direction of this sentence. His character is the premise of the cross: if He had owed a debt Himself, He could not have paid for others. And the cross is the purpose of His character: on the road He stopped for the person with leprosy, and in the end He stopped there for the whole world. So the place we go in the next unit is Golgotha.
Spiritual meaning: from self-centered to selfless

The Bible is our standard, and Jesus is our example. But an example is not for us to imitate through gritted teeth; gritted teeth only make us prouder or more discouraged. The real change is that “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” To move from self-centered to selfless is to let this flawless Lord, bit by bit, reign in our tempers, our calendars and our speech.

This week’s homework is simple: find one person you see every day but have never really looked at. A building security guard, a cleaning lady or a colleague’s assistant will do. Ask for their name, remember it, and call them by it next time. You will find that stopping for thirty seconds is harder than you think, and more like Jesus than you think.

To the friends who have not yet come to faith, thank you for listening this far. I will not ask you to agree to anything today. If, reading the Gospels, you feel there is something He did wrong, you are welcome to come and argue with me. That is how He asked in the first place: who can convict me? That question is still open today.

Please be quiet for a moment and think about which part of you is the part you assume He would not want to touch. Lord Jesus, You stopped to see the ones people passed over, and You saw me. My goodness cannot last through a single meal, yet You were made sin for me. Forgive me, and change me by Your Spirit, so that I treat people the way You treat me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Of the scenes in the Gospels of how Jesus treated people, which moves you most? Which makes you most uncomfortable? Please share honestly.
2. Of Russell’s three charges, which do you find hardest to answer? If a friend asked you, how would you begin, and what would you admit you are also unsure about?
3. Think of your most recent anger: was it because someone was being kept outside the door, or because of your own face? In whom do you want to learn to “stop” this week?
The Cross: Why Did He Have to Die?
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Let me ask you to picture a scene. You walk into a church, and on the roof stands a gallows. The bride walks in with a tiny golden noose around her neck, and everyone thinks it looks beautiful. You would probably start quietly edging toward the door, making a mental note of where the exit is.

Yet we do exactly this every week. We have just gotten used to it. We turn the cross into necklaces, neon signs and car stickers, and sometimes the neon sign is half burned out. We are so used to it that we no longer hear how strange it is. Today I want to take that habit away and ask together a very old and very direct question: why did He have to die?
We will take three steps today. First, history: what was the cross in those days? Then the Bible: why did He go up there? And finally, a very sharp accusation: isn’t this a father abusing his son?
One: the word Romans would not say
The donkey head on the wall

On the Palatine Hill in Rome there was once a room where someone had scratched a graffito into the wall plaster with a sharp point. It showed a figure with a donkey’s head hanging on a cross, and beside it stood a man with his hand raised. Underneath, in crooked Greek letters, were the words: Alexamenos worships his god. The graffito was unearthed in 1857, and scholars are still debating its date, most often placing it somewhere between the second and third centuries. It is generally taken to be someone laughing at him. Imagine that man Alexamenos walking into the room the next day and seeing that picture on the wall. That is probably what it felt like to be a Christian back then.

Why was it funny? Because in those days the cross was the dirtiest word there was. In the first century BC the Roman advocate Cicero, in one lawsuit, accused a governor of crucifying a man who kept crying out, “I am a Roman citizen,” and described this punishment as the most cruel and terrible. In another speech he even argued that the very name of the cross should stay far away not only from the body of a Roman citizen but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears.

The German scholar Martin Hengel wrote a slim classic in 1977 that gathers up this history. This punishment was mostly used on slaves and the lower classes, and it was deliberately carried out where people passed by. The whole point was to tell everyone: do not turn out like him. And almost no one in the ancient world wrote against it. It is as if, along the highway today, every so often there were a man hanging there breathing his last, and everyone just drove past and kept listening to the radio.

Archaeology has left a trace too. In 1968, in a tomb northeast of Jerusalem, the remains of a first-century man were dug up. His name was Yehohanan, and an iron nail was still lodged through his heel bone. The details of this find have been revised several times since. Even the length of the nail has been given different figures, and that is honest scholarship. Brothers and sisters, the cross in the Gospels is not a symbol. Those were real nails through real bone.
For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. (1 Corinthians 1:18)
Spiritual meaning: this is what we preach

Paul knew perfectly well how harsh this sounded. He said it was a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles. If you were inventing a religion to attract Romans, you would never choose this emblem. It would be like a start-up designing its logo as an electric chair. The early Christians did not hide it. They put it right at the center of the message. That alone is worth asking about: why?
Two: why He went up there

The historical answer is very clear. The one who gave the order was the Roman governor Pilate, and the sign on the cross read “the King of the Jews,” a political charge. The Roman historian Tacitus also mentions that Christ was put to death by Pilate during the reign of Tiberius. The Gospels also record that some of the religious leaders of the time took part. Let me say one thing plainly here: some in history have used this to pin the guilt on the whole Jewish people, and it has done enormous harm. That is wrong, and we must clearly reject it. Jesus Himself was a Jew.
The Bible’s answer is more unsettling, because it counts us in.

But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. (Isaiah 53:5-6)

The New Testament does not hand us a formula. It gives us several photographs, like photographing Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain, from different directions. The first is substitution: what I deserved, He bore. It answers one question: how can a righteous God forgive people instead of pretending nothing happened? If a judge said “never mind” to every evil, the first to object would be the victims’ families. The second is victory: through His death He defeated the powers of sin and death. The Swedish theologian Aulén held that this was the main theme of the church’s first thousand years. The third is the call of love: the cross lets people see God’s heart, and they melt. The fourth is reconciliation: tearing down the walls between people and God, and between people and one another.

The evangelical tradition gives particular weight to the first photograph, and I lean on it deeply myself. But we do not have to tear up the other three in order to hold on to one. A person bound in darkness needs a Lord who wins the victory. A person carrying a debt of sin needs a Lord who pays in their place. A person with a hard heart needs to be melted by that love.

Let me give a comparison. A judge sentences you to a fine you cannot pay, and when the sentence is finished he takes off his robe, steps down, and pays it for you. Justice is not discounted, and mercy is real. Of course this picture has limits, and we will get to them in a moment.

Friends often ask: God is God, so why doesn’t He just forgive? Why all this bloodshed? I think that is a good question too. But think about it. A friend runs off with half a million of your money, and you decide to forgive him. Where did the half million go? It does not vanish into thin air. You swallowed it yourself. Real forgiveness is never free; the one who forgives simply picks up the bill. That is true of human debts, and even more true of the harm people do to God and to one another. The cross shows us that God did not make the victim swallow it for nothing, and He did not make us pay what we cannot pay. He took the bill on Himself.

Look at the order Paul gives: “While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” He did not wait until you quit smoking, repaired your marriage and gave enough in the offering. We are good at calculating. We even want to buy heaven on an installment plan. The cross snatched away the calculator and left only one sentence: it has already been paid. Humility overcomes pride, and it begins with admitting that I cannot pay.

Please listen carefully to this next part. In 1989 two women theologians, Brown and Parker, brought a charge from the situation of abuse survivors: if God’s redemption is a father letting his son suffer, should beaten children and beaten wives also silently endure? In 2003 a British evangelical pastor, Steve Chalke, also wrote that if substitution is told as a vengeful father punishing an innocent son, it is “cosmic child abuse.”

Brothers and sisters, this is not idle nitpicking. There is blood and tears in it. I must admit that people in the church have actually said to abused sisters, “You have to carry your cross,” and that sentence has hurt people. So let me say it plainly here today: if you are suffering domestic violence or abuse, Jesus does not ask you to stay there. Seek safety, find professional help, find someone you can trust. Carrying the cross is a free act of love. It does not mean that when someone hits you, you may not run.
The Father and the Son came together

So is the accusation right? The evangelical scholar Garry Williams answered in 2007. First, Jesus was not a helpless child. He was an adult with a mature will. In Gethsemane He prayed, “let this cup pass away from me,” and His anguish was real; yet He also said this.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.” (John 10:18)

Second, the Trinity is not one angry God and a poor third party. That is where the judge picture has its limit: the One on the cross was not a third party outside God. It was the Son of God, who Himself came down. The Bible says that “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself”; the sending and the self-giving are two sides of one love. Romans 5:8 does not say God’s anger is displayed here. It says God “commends his own love toward us.” I will not claim that this unlocks the whole mystery, and I cannot unlock it either. But an abuser pushes pain onto someone else, while on the cross God Himself walked into the pain. The two run in opposite directions.
Spiritual meaning: He did not come down

That day the people below shouted loudly: “save yourself, and come down from the cross!” They thought it was the perfect test.
