Brothers and sisters, when He was arrested He said He could ask the Father to send “more than twelve legions of angels.” He could have come down. He did not. What kept Him up there was not the nails. It was love. And the story did not stop on Friday. We will look at that tomb in our next unit. The resurrection tells us that execution was in fact a victory.

This is why Paul could say, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Going from self-centered to selfless is not gritting our teeth and suppressing ourselves. It is discovering that Someone has already died for me, so I no longer have to prove myself in order to live. Letting Jesus receive all the glory begins right here.

This week, I ask you to do one thing: write on a sheet of paper one piece of guilt you have carried for a long time, pray about it to God, read 1 John 1:9, and then tear the paper up. If it involves someone you owe an apology or restitution, talk with a spiritual companion about the next step.

To friends who have not yet come to faith, thank you for listening all the way to here. If you are thinking today, I don’t know whether I believe, but if this were true, that love would be enormous, I want to tell you that this is a very good beginning. You do not need to decide today, but please keep investigating.

Let us be quiet, and bring to mind the thing you are most ashamed of. Lord Jesus, You stayed there for me. I no longer have to buy Your love with my performance, and I no longer have to pretend I have no sin. I bring this to Your cross. Thank You for forgiving me, and from today make me die to myself and live to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. When did you first truly feel the meaning of the cross? Or have you still not felt it? Please share honestly either way.
2. Of the four photographs (substitution, victory, the call of love, reconciliation), which one hits your situation right now? Which one is hardest for you to accept?
3. What real pain lies behind the accusation of “cosmic child abuse”? If a friend who had been abused asked you this, how would you first be present with them, and then answer?
The Empty Tomb: A Question Mark That Frightened Everyone
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruit of those who are asleep. (1 Corinthians 15:20)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! If anyone wanted to overthrow Christianity, Paul wrote the instruction manual nearly two thousand years ago. It has only one step: prove that Jesus did not rise. He did not ask anyone to go easy on him, and he did not say “just feeling it in your heart is enough.” He put it straight into a letter.
If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith also is in vain. (1 Corinthians 15:14)

Think about it: what company would write in its product manual, “If this part does not exist, please throw away everything we make”? Paul wrote exactly that. So today we have come to the most important room in Jesus Hall, and we stand before a tomb.

Let me set the ground rules for today. Many skeptical scholars have studied this tomb seriously, and I will state their strongest arguments without discounting them. I will also tell you which things you often hear that you should stop using. The Lord we believe in does not need us to water anything down for Him.
One: a list sealed in amber
What Paul handed on is older than his letter

Have you ever seen amber? A small insect sealed in honey-colored resin. You pick it up at a market today, but the insect lived tens of millions of years ago. 1 Corinthians 15 holds a piece of amber like that.

For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, (1 Corinthians 15:3-4)

Paul wrote this letter in about the 50s AD, more than twenty years after the cross. But he says he “received” these words, so the sentences inside are older than the letter. How much older? The New Testament scholar James Dunn holds that it took shape within a few months of Jesus’ death. The German scholar Gerd Lüdemann, who does not believe in the resurrection, also says within the first two years. Others caution against figuring it too precisely; Ehrman says that earlier than Paul’s letter does not mean earlier than his conversion. Most scholars still hold that its source lies only a few years from the event.

What does the amber tell us? It tells us that these people were preaching this very early, and that the resurrection was not an idea that grew up several generations later. What can the amber not tell us? It cannot decide for us that what they said was true. Please remember that distinction.
Spiritual meaning: faith can be investigated

Brothers and sisters, many questions of faith are afraid of being asked, but on this one Paul himself put it on the table and invited people to check. That gives us great freedom: when your child asks you, when a coworker asks you, you do not need to be anxious, and you do not need to pretend to know everything. You can say, “Good question, let’s look into it together.” The Bible is my standard, and a standard is not afraid of being opened.
Two: three clues at the tomb, and three objections
The first clue is a recognizable tomb.

Mark is very specific: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, went to Pilate to ask for the body, laid Jesus in a tomb cut out of rock, and the women saw where He was placed. The archaeologist Jodi Magness considers such a description consistent with burial practice in Jerusalem at that time. The scholar John Granger Cook, after reviewing the ancient sources, also says that crucified people were occasionally buried by family or by people concerned with the burial.

Now the second, a group of witnesses who were the worst possible casting. All four Gospels put women at the tomb. In those days that earned no points at all. When the Jewish historian Josephus restates the law, he says women are not to give testimony, on the ground that they are frivolous. The second-century critic of Christianity Celsus was even blunter, in effect: who saw it? A half-hysterical woman, that’s who.

If you were looking for a spokesperson for a new drug today, you would pick the head of a medical center, not someone everyone says cannot be believed. The scholars Richard Bauckham and Dale Allison both think real memory was most likely preserved here. But let us not overstate it: a courtroom rule is not the same as everyday life in which women were never listened to.

The third clue is the opponents’ reply. Matthew himself records what was being said outside: the disciples stole the body by night. Justin Martyr in the second century mentions the same charge. The opponents were explaining where the body went. But the force of this clue is limited; it does not mean the opponents ever went to the tomb to examine it.

Now the other side comes on, so please sit tight. Bart Ehrman of the University of North Carolina: I have boiled his argument down to four statements. First, the cross was meant to humiliate and deter, so why would the Romans hand a man condemned for rebellion to his friends for an honorable burial? He estimates the body was most likely handled hastily. Crossan also argues that the disciples did not actually know what became of the body. Second, the Joseph story comes mainly from Mark, Matthew and Luke most likely copied it, and Paul’s creed does not mention Joseph either.

Third, Paul’s letters do not explicitly say the tomb was empty, and the earliest narrative appears in Mark, nearly forty years later. The scholar Richard Carrier argues that the earliest believers were talking about a spiritual body, and that the empty tomb was a later legend. Fourth, the details differ among the Gospels: Mark speaks of a young man, Luke of two men; and Mark 16:8 even ends with the women saying nothing to anyone.

Brothers and sisters, these are not the words of ignorant people. Do believing scholars have a reply? Yes. The creed’s sequence is died, buried, raised, so the one who was buried rising naturally implies the body is no longer in the tomb; and differences in detail may be just the trace of many people retelling it independently. But I must tell you honestly that this discussion is not closed.
Spiritual meaning: please put down that 75%

On the internet you often see a line: “75% of scholars accept the empty tomb.” The source is a 2005 article by Habermas, himself an evangelical scholar, who worked hard to read more than 1,400 publications. But he himself says it is only a rough estimate, an informal barometer, and he states plainly that this proportion cannot prove the resurrection. It is one person’s compilation of publications, not a poll, and critics also point out that the raw data was never made public.

So when you share the gospel, please do not wave this number at people. Truth is not decided by a show of hands. Please also stop using the Nazareth Inscription: a 2020 study indicated that the marble came from the Greek island of Kos, and the inscription does not mention Jesus. We are willing to pull out the nails one by one, because humility overcomes pride, even in the middle of apologetics.
Three: the question mark and the call
The empty tomb could not convince Mary
By now you may think that once the tomb is proved empty, the matter is settled. Look at the first eyewitness. She came while it was still dark, and saw the stone rolled away. What was her conclusion?
“They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!” (John 20:2)

She reported a theft! Ehrman is right on this point: an empty tomb by itself does not produce faith. Luke also writes that when the women went back with the news, the apostles took it for nonsense. Professor Wright, who has studied how Jews two thousand years ago understood resurrection, also holds that the empty tomb and the appearances must be taken together, and that without either one neither can be explained. So the empty tomb is a question mark.
The One who calls by name
How does a question mark become a period? Mary stood outside the tomb weeping, and even when Jesus stood right in front of her she took Him for the gardener. He said just one word.
Jesus said to her, “Mary.”She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!” (John 20:16)

Brothers and sisters, when you hear someone in a crowd call you in the tone only family uses, you do not need to check any ID; your spine knows. History can accompany us as far as the door of the tomb. What turns a person around from the tomb is a personal meeting with the living Lord.
Spiritual meaning: what kind of God is He?

Here we need to be clear about the layers. Whether the tomb was empty is a historical question; it depends on evidence and can be argued. That God raised Jesus from the dead is a confession of faith, and also what we hold to be the best explanation; the historical method by itself cannot render this verdict.

But once we believe that sentence, what kind of God do we see? He is faithful: the Son who was condemned and thrown into death, He did not abandon. He is almighty: Acts says “it was not possible that he should be held by it.” Some of you have just said goodbye to a loved one, and I will not give you a lecture. I will only tell you that Paul calls Christ the “first fruit.” When the first one ripens, it means a whole field is still to come. The Lord sees your tears, and He remembers your longing.

Chinese people understand tombs. When Qingming comes, the whole family drives up the mountain with buckets and fresh flowers, crouches down to pull weeds, and talks to the headstone. We go to the grave because someone we love lies there. This is exactly how those women felt early that morning: they carried spices to anoint a body, and on the way they were still worrying about who would help move the stone. Not one of them set out expecting, “Today the Lord will rise.” Like us, they were going to sweep a grave. The shock of that morning began there and has reached all the way to today.

Brothers and sisters, in 321 we often say that when our mindset changes, our lives change. From the human, temporary point of view, the tomb is the end; everyone arrives there, and no one comes out again. From God’s eternal point of view, there is one tomb that could not hold the One inside, and so other tombs no longer have the last word.

To friends who are still investigating: today I do not ask you to believe at once. Please read Mark 16 and John 20 for yourself, mark the similarities and differences in two colors, and then bring your biggest question. If you want to ask, you can also say directly to Jesus: “If You are really alive, call my name.”

Risen Lord, thank You for not staying in the tomb. My faith is often like Mary’s: I see, but I do not understand. Call my name, so that I turn around and recognize You. Comfort those who today are missing someone who has died, and let us know that the tomb door is not the last word. Reign in our lives, and may all the glory go to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Of Ehrman’s four objections, which one makes you feel you need to think again? Why might hearing the strongest objection actually be good for faith?

2. Mary saw the empty tomb yet thought the body had been moved, until Jesus called her name. Have you had a “hearing your name” experience? How could you share it with an unbelieving friend without pressure?
3. If a friend asks you next week, “Don’t 75% of scholars accept the empty tomb?”, how would you answer honestly? Practice it with one another.
The Disciples’ Transformation: The Door That Opened From the Inside
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus. (Acts 4:13)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Picture a door. Not the gate of a mansion, but a perfectly ordinary wooden door in some house in Jerusalem. That night the door was shut from the inside. There were a dozen or so grown men in the house, talking in low voices, and whenever footsteps sounded outside they all stopped breathing together.
Their teacher had been nailed up by the Romans just three days before. They had followed Him for three years, and now each of them had only one question in his head: am I next?

When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle and said to them, “Peace be to you.” (John 20:19)

All right, fast-forward about seven weeks. Same city, same people in power. One of them stands up in front of everyone and says loudly: listen to me, all of you. Who? Peter. The same Peter who, in the high priest’s courtyard, could not hold up under the questioning of a single servant girl.

Here is the question history has to answer: what happened in those seven weeks? Today we will not rush to a conclusion. We will investigate together, and also see what it has to do with the door that we ourselves keep shut.
One: Peter, from the charcoal fire to the council
The Bible does not put makeup on its leaders

If you were founding a religion and needed a founder as your signboard, how would you write him? Probably as wise and mighty. But when the Gospels write about Peter, they write in a way that makes you feel embarrassed for him. Jesus had only just said that he would fall, and he thumped his chest and promised he never would. A few hours later someone recognized him, and he swore with curses.

But he began to curse and to swear, “I don’t know this man of whom you speak!”The rooster crowed the second time. Peter remembered the words that Jesus said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” When he thought about that, he wept. (Mark 14:71-72)
The first seat in the church left a record like this, and it has been passed down for two thousand years. If this were a company website, the PR department would have deleted it long ago.
The same man, a different man

Then we come to Acts chapter 4, where Peter and John are arrested and brought before the council, the very circle of power that had just condemned Jesus. They were warned not to speak the name of Jesus any more. How did Peter answer? “we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”

Notice how the text describes them: the council saw that they were “unlearned and ignorant men.” That is not flattering, but it is honest. Peter had not gone to a famous school, and he had not suddenly earned a degree. His head was still a fisherman’s head, but he was no longer afraid.

But let us also be honest: he did not become perfect from then on. Paul records in Galatians that Peter later, out of fear of what people would think, drew back once again at Antioch. I like that account very much, because it is reassuring: the people God uses are real people, not bronze statues.
Spiritual meaning: He did not replace him

What could Jesus have done with Peter after the resurrection? He could have fired him, replaced him with someone steadier, held a review meeting. He did none of those. He lit a fire by the sea, cooked breakfast, and asked him about his love three times. Each time He asked, He handed him a work of shepherding.

Brothers and sisters, perhaps you have something you have hidden for many years, and you feel God will probably never use you again. Today remember that charcoal fire. Three denials answered by three questions: that is the Lord’s arithmetic.
Two: James, the audience hardest to persuade
The hardest younger brother in the world

The second figure I especially want to introduce is Jesus’ younger brother James. Brothers and sisters, if you want to know whether a person is really great, do not ask his fans; ask his family. Fans see the stage. Family saw how he looked when he was scolded as a child.

The Bible honestly tells us that during Jesus’ ministry His family did not buy it. Mark 3:21 says, “When his friends heard it, they went out to seize him; for they said, ‘He is insane.’” (The Chinese Union Version says “relatives” where this reads “friends.”) John 7:5 also says that even His brothers did not believe in Him.

Imagine your older brother saying at dinner one evening: I am the Savior all humanity has been waiting for. What would you do? I would guess you would put down your chopsticks and ask Mom where the health insurance card is. That was about the atmosphere in James’s home.
A line from an outside historian

But what happened later? In Paul’s own letter to the Galatians he calls him “James, the Lord’s brother,” one of the pillars of the church. There is almost no dispute among scholars about who wrote that letter.

Even more interesting is the record from outside the church. The Jewish historian Josephus, who was not a Christian, records in Book 20 of the Antiquities that around AD 62 the Roman governor died and the new governor was still on his way, leaving a power vacuum. The high priest Ananus took the chance to hand over James, the brother of Jesus, and have him stoned to death. Josephus’s wording is “who was called Christ,” in a very neutral tone, and that is one reason most scholars consider the passage reliable.
From “he is out of his mind” to being stoned without changing his story, what happened in between? What Paul passes on is only a handful of words.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, (1 Corinthians 15:7)
Spiritual meaning: change shows at the closest range

This is a very practical reminder for us. Outsiders see our pulpit; people at home see our temper. Whether your faith is real, your wife knows, your son knows, and your coworkers probably know too. In the 321 framework we often say that every relationship is my “two,” and the fruit of life has to grow in these relationships. It waits for the day your family says: this person really is different.
Three: what can martyrdom prove, and what can it not?
First, let us say it accurately
Now I want to ask you to do something: adjust a line you often hear. Many sermons say that all twelve apostles except John were martyred. That goes too far.

The American scholar Sean McDowell wrote a whole study called The Fate of the Apostles. He is a Christian himself, but he assesses very honestly: Peter, Paul, James son of Zebedee, and James the Lord’s brother have the strongest evidence; for Thomas and Andrew the likelihood is moderate; for many others the sources are late and contradictory, and all we can say is that we do not know; and for John he thinks a natural death is most likely.

Skeptical scholars are more reserved still. Ehrman thinks the sources are actually few. Tacitus records Nero executing Christians, so the martyrdom of Peter and Paul is a reasonable inference; details such as Peter being crucified upside down are legends from more than a hundred years later. 1 Clement, from around AD 95, mentions their suffering and witness, but does not say how they died. We who share the gospel must dare to say all of this clearly. Exaggerate in one place, and people will doubt the whole.
Sincere is not the same as correct

So what does martyrdom prove? Brothers and sisters, it cannot prove that Christianity is true. People of every faith in the world have been willing to die for it, and they were sincere too, and we should respect that. McDowell himself says so.

What it can show is that these people were not liars. A liar may deceive you for money, or deceive you for fame, but very few people take stones for a story they themselves know to be false. They may have been mistaken, and we will discuss that carefully in the next unit; but the road of “they knew it was false” is very hard to travel.
It is like a signed guarantee. The signature cannot prove the contents are one hundred percent correct, but it tells you the person who signed meant it.
Spiritual meaning: power is not squeezed out

So where did the courage of these timid men come from? The Bible’s answer comes in two parts: they saw the risen Lord, and they received the Holy Spirit. This is a confession of faith. History cannot prove it for us, and I will not pretend it can. But I ask you to notice that the disciples’ own account of the matter is quite consistent: the power was not their own.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

Many Christians strain to squeeze out courage, like squeezing the last of the toothpaste, and the more they squeeze the more tired they get. Acts gives a different method: wait first, receive first. Humility overcomes pride, and it starts here. Peter once relied on his own resolve and fell three times; later he said, “Lord, you know everything,” and relied on the Lord. No longer I, but Christ lives in me.

Brothers and sisters, is there a door shut in your heart today? Perhaps it is a past you are afraid people will find out, perhaps a sentence you have never dared say to your family, perhaps a wish to share the gospel that never gets past your lips. Jesus came into a house where the door was shut, stood in the middle, and His first words were “Peace be to you.” No rebuke. No naming of names.

To friends who have not yet come to faith: today I am not asking you to believe because others died. I only ask you to think seriously about one question: what was it that turned this group of men from hiding indoors into walking out into the street? Please investigate it for yourself.

This week I ask you to do one small thing: find someone you have let down, or who has let you down, and write one sincere line of greeting or apology. If that relationship has brought harm or danger, you do not need to force contact; bring it to God first and find a trusted person to walk with you.

Risen Lord, like Peter I have made big promises, and I have also drawn back. Thank You for not replacing me. May Your Spirit live in me and open the door I have kept shut in my heart, so that I no longer depend on my own courage but on Your presence. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Peter’s failures are preserved in the Bible. How does that help you understand the faith? Have you had a failure that later became a comfort to someone else?
2. Why is family the hardest witness to persuade? What do you most easily show at home? What is one concrete thing you could change this week?
3. How do you react to hearing that “not all twelve apostles were necessarily martyred”? Why does honesty matter more than eloquence when we share the gospel?
Other Explanations for the Resurrection: Trying Every Key Once
When they saw him, they bowed down to him; but some doubted. (Matthew 28:17)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! If tonight's news reported that someone had died, stayed dead three days, and come back to life, I would ask you to doubt it. Really, please doubt it. If you did not doubt, I would be the one to worry about you, because next week someone might sell you a bottle of resurrection health supplements.
Scripture not only permits this doubt, it recorded it with its own hand. Who were the first to hear the news of the resurrection? The apostles. What was their reaction?
These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them. (Luke 24:11)

“Nonsense” would today be something like “you’re just overtired.” And at the end of Matthew, Jesus has risen and the disciples see Him, the very climax of the whole book, yet Matthew adds precisely the line “but some doubted.” If this were a press release, a supervisor would have circled that line in red long ago.

In the last unit we left a question: the disciples’ transformation was real and their sincerity is hard to deny, but sincere people can also be mistaken. So today I invite the other side onto the stage. I will state their explanations until even they nod, and then we will look together at where they stick. The first thing we need to learn is this: honesty matters more than winning.
One: three of the older keys

Let me first give you a picture. Imagine a door with four locks. The first lock: the tomb was empty. The second: Peter and the others were convinced they had seen Jesus. The third: Paul, a persecutor of the church, turned around. The fourth: James, the younger brother who had not believed, also turned around. Every explanation is a key, and we are going to try them.

The first key: stolen body. This is the oldest one, and Matthew already records it. The 18th-century German scholar Reimarus argued that the disciples stole the body and hid it to keep the resurrection claim alive. The difficulty is that knowing it was fake and still being willing to lose everything is psychologically very hard to sustain. The harder version to refute is that the body was moved by other people, without the disciples knowing. But that opens only the first lock, and the other three stay shut.

The second key: the swoon. Jesus did not actually die and revived in the cool of the tomb. This view was very popular in the early 19th century. What knocked it down was not a pastor but a scholar who did not believe in the resurrection, Strauss. His argument is a clever one: imagine a man who has been tortured, covered in wounds, needing help to walk, crawling to the disciples. What would they say? They would probably say, “Call an ambulance!” They would not say, “Death has been conquered!” A person like that makes you feel sympathy, not worship. By the end of the 19th century scholars had mostly abandoned this view.

The third key: the wrong tomb. In 1907 Lake proposed that, before dawn, in a strange city, and grieving, the women may well have gone to the wrong place. Don’t laugh, brothers and sisters; our own family has gone to the wrong grave at tomb-sweeping time and bowed for a good while to someone else’s ancestors. But Mark says they had seen where He was laid. More importantly, as soon as one person went to the right tomb, the whole matter would be over. This key also touches only the first lock.
Spiritual meaning: don’t rush to laugh at someone else’s key

Brothers and sisters, these explanations sound a bit weak now, but in their day they were seriously thought out by clever people. They were willing to face the question, and that deserves more respect than the many who only say “praise the Lord” and have never thought about it. Scripture says to answer everyone “with humility and fear,” and that applies even when we are right.
Two: the two strongest keys today

I want you to listen carefully to this next one. The German scholar Lüdemann and the American scholar Ehrman both hold that Peter, in extreme grief and guilt, saw a vision of Jesus, and that it spread from one person to ten and from ten to a hundred, until others had similar experiences.

Don’t rush to object. In 1971 the British physician Rees interviewed widows and widowers in mid-Wales, and about 14% said they had seen their deceased spouse, and nearly half had sensed the spouse’s presence. I believe some of you have experienced it, sensing in the middle of the night that your husband or wife was still sitting by the bed. It is not madness. It is love that goes deep, and it is a common experience of the bereaved. Pastors, when someone tells you about this, never say that they are possessed.

So this key really does turn in the second lock. The difficulty comes after. First, when Jews saw a vision of the dead, the usual conclusion was “his soul is still around,” and Professor Wright’s research stresses that they would not therefore say “he has been raised.” Second, Paul was not in the circle of grief; he was carrying papers to arrest people. James had also not believed at first. Third, there is the record of more than five hundred people. But Professor Allison, who has studied this more deeply than anyone, also cautions that we know very little about the five hundred, and that “he appeared to the twelve” does not mean each had the same experience. So this question is not closed.
Later legend, and two keys at once

Next is legend. Stories grow in the telling, and that is quite reasonable. When my grandfather caught a fish, it grew one centimeter with every Lunar New Year. The details in the four Gospels do differ, and that is where Ehrman starts. But legend can explain why the fish got bigger, only if someone had gone fishing in the first place. Paul himself says he saw Peter and James, and that list is so early, so legend itself cannot answer where the original conviction came from.

The other side has one more strong move, and I will state it for them: why must there be only one key? A body moved by someone, plus grief visions, plus later legend: why can’t all three open it together? Brothers and sisters, that is reasonable. Many apologetics books have not faced this move seriously. What we can say is that after combining them, each key has to hold exactly, and they have to fit together exactly, and the probability of that has to be calculated too. But that is not the same as refuting it.

Some friends will also bring out a newer key called cognitive dissonance. In 1956 the psychologist Festinger wrote When Prophecy Fails, recording a small group waiting for the end of the world, in which some believers, after the prophecy failed, became even more zealous in spreading their message. Might the disciples be the same? The teacher died, they couldn’t bear it, so they believed all the harder. The analogy is attractive. But two things need noting. First, this classic itself has recently run into trouble: Thomas Kelly, working from the archives, charges that its central claim contains fabrication and exaggeration. Second, let us not be too quick to cheer: one analogy failing does not mean the resurrection is established. It is the same on both sides: do not treat a popular analogy as settled.
Spiritual meaning: even Jesus let Thomas finish first
See how difficult Thomas was. He set a condition: unless I touch the nail marks, I will never believe. When Jesus came back, the first thing He did was to follow his condition.

Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:27-28)

He did not shame him. And what He stretched out was a hand with nail marks. The risen Lord still carries the mark of the cross, a detail even a novelist would not easily think of. That wound was received for Thomas. When we face doubting friends, we too should reach out the hand first and speak afterward.
Three: the last door, do you allow God on the table?
The problem is not the sources

By now you will have noticed that the argument has left the sources behind. The 18th-century philosopher Hume argued that we should not believe a miracle unless the falseness of the testimony would be more incredible than the miracle. A dead man coming back to life is certainly extremely incredible. Later philosophers revised him and criticized him, but the question he asked is the right one.
Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead? (Acts 26:8)

This sentence of Paul’s lays bare the heart of the matter. If from the very start you take the key called “God” off the table, then any natural explanation, however strained, beats the resurrection. If God exists, raising the dead is no difficulty for Him. So this judgment depends not only on the sources but on how you see the world. Let me say it clearly: an honest and wise atheist, looking at the same data, can reach a different conclusion. We should not say they have bad motives; we should respect them.

Here are a few examples that make things more interesting. The Jewish scholar Lapide wrote a whole book on the resurrection of Jesus, treating it as an experience of Jewish faith, yet he did not therefore acknowledge Jesus as Israel’s Messiah. Professor Allison, who has studied it most deeply, also does not claim that visions explain everything; he says that apologists and skeptics both cannot do what they claim. Licona holds that historians may list the resurrection as the best explanation, while many historians think this goes beyond the tools of history. You see, there is no simple dividing line here: the clever people are not all on the other side, nor all on this side.
But we cannot help asking. Paul himself staked everything he had on this.
If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith also is in vain. (1 Corinthians 15:14)
An apostle wrote to the church: if this is false, you need not believe any more. This sentence is not meant to frighten. It is an invitation, an invitation to investigate.
Spiritual meaning: three reactions, and a path for each

When Paul spoke about the resurrection in Athens, he got three reactions: some mocked, some said they would hear him again another time, and a few believed. To the friend who says “another time,” please know that this is a very good place to be. You do not have to decide today. But please investigate seriously, because if this is true, it changes everything.

Brothers and sisters, today we have not defeated anyone. There is no benefit in out-arguing your friend; he will only be more hurt and more unwilling to listen. In 321 we say that people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Let us move from self-centered to selfless: I do not need to be the one who is always right; I only need to point to the One who truly has the victory.

This week I ask you to do one assignment: find an article or video written by a skeptic, watch or read it through carefully, and write down one point where you think he has a case. Then go and ask your friend: what do you think is the most reasonable explanation? And listen until he has finished.

Please take out a sheet of paper and write down your most honest doubt, without polishing it, and come to prayer with it. Lord Jesus, thank You for not leaving Thomas because of his doubt. I bring my questions to You. Show Yourself to me in Your own way, and give me a gentle and reverent heart toward friends who are still doubting. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Of the five keys, which do you find the strongest? If it were true, what effect would it have on your faith? Please share honestly.
2. The bereaved often have the experience of sensing the presence of the dead. If someone told you this, how would you respond so that you are first present with them, and only then explain?
3. Do you have a friend who is in the state of “we want to hear you again concerning this”? This week, how could you accompany him rather than hurry him?
Paul’s Conversion: The Wanted Man Takes the Pulpit

For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. (1 Corinthians 15:9-10)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Suppose that next week your church receives a notice saying that a certain brother is coming to preach. You look at the name and your hands begin to shake. Last year this man led a crowd into your friend’s home and dragged husband and wife off to prison, and when someone was stoned to death, he stood by and watched. Now the notice says that his topic will be “Jesus is Lord.” Brothers and sisters, which row would you sit in? I would guess you would sit near the door, and first make sure where your children are.

This is not a movie plot. It is news from the first century, and we have the man’s own handwriting. The one we look at today is Saul, later called Paul. Last time we looked at other explanations and at the disciples’ transformation. This time we look at a man who started out standing on the other side.
but they only heard, “He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy.”So they glorified God in me. (Galatians 1:23-24)
Today I want to remind you: do not tell Paul’s story as a success manual. He could not explain it himself. We also need to separate what is certain from what is uncertain.
One: the résumé in his own hand

First, something that matters a great deal for verification. Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry Paul’s name, and scholars almost unanimously accept seven of them as his own: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. The authorship of the others is disputed, and I will be honest about that in a moment.

These seven letters are like registered-mail evidence. Professor Sanders, a leading authority on Paul, in his entry for the Encyclopaedia Britannica argues that to know Paul we should rely mainly on these letters, and that Acts is a useful secondary source. That matters a great deal to us. We do not need to rely on legends from a hundred years later; he confessed it himself in his letters.

For you have heard of my way of living in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it. I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. (Galatians 1:13-14)
Not a troublemaker, a top student

Please notice that he did not come to faith because he had nowhere else to turn. The format of many testimonies today is: I used to take drugs and gamble, my life hit rock bottom, and then I met the Lord. Thank God, those testimonies are precious. But Paul’s version is: I was first in the class. In Philippians he lists his résumé: circumcised on the eighth day, a Pharisee, so zealous that he persecuted the church, and “concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.”

That sentence is inconvenient for a popular explanation. Some suppose he was already full of guilt and broke down because he could not bear it. Is that possible? No one can rule it out. But his own words do not read that way. Professor Stendahl, in a very famous 1963 essay, warns us that reading Paul as a conscience-sick man lying awake at night may be something Westerners added later.
Spiritual meaning: good people need the gospel too

This is an important word for many second-generation church members and many earnest good people. You can be very well behaved, very zealous, serve in church for twenty years, and still be walking in the opposite direction. When Saul was most zealous, that was when he hurt God’s people most deeply. Pride does not always look like a thug. Sometimes it wears holy clothes.
Two: what happened on the road?

Now the thing everyone most wants to know. Acts records that as he neared Damascus a light came from heaven, he fell to the ground, and he heard a voice. Acts tells this story three times, and the details are not identical. Chapter 9 says the men traveling with him heard the sound but saw no one; chapter 22 says they saw the light but did not understand the voice. Paul’s own letters are much shorter, saying only that God was pleased “to reveal his Son in me.”

Should we be nervous? No. We lay these differences on the table. Ancient authors telling the same event three times naturally varied, and interpreters have different ways of harmonizing them. But we should not pretend not to see them. That is the attitude of verification.

The first: the risen Jesus really appeared to him, and that is how Paul himself understood it. In 1 Corinthians he put himself last in the list of witnesses to the resurrection: “and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.” The second: the German scholar Lüdemann and others hold that this was a real subjective vision, not an external event. The third is a psychological explanation, like the guilt theory we just mentioned.

I want to be very fair. What history can confirm is that this man’s direction was reversed, and that he believed he had seen the Lord. What he saw, historical method cannot answer with a hundred percent certainty. If you believe there is a God, the first explanation will feel natural; if you do not, you will lean toward the second or third. An honest atheist friend can disagree after looking, and we respect him. But I would ask him to think about one thing with us: what makes a person willing to give up his future, and then be whipped, jailed, shipwrecked, all the way to old age?

Are they servants of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself.) I am more so: in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, and in deaths often. Five times I received forty stripes minus one from the Jews. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I have been a night and a day in the deep. (2 Corinthians 11:23-25)

Of course, being willing to pay a price only proves he was sincere, not that he was right. We said that in an earlier unit. But this list holds another point worth noticing. Professor Fredriksen points out that synagogue floggings were inflicted only on Jews. His five floggings mean he stayed within that community and was still preaching in the synagogues. Scholars therefore discuss whether to call him “converted” or “called.” He did not change gods; he came to know the One sent by the God he had always worshiped. Bishop Wright’s conclusion is interesting: in one sense a calling, and in another sense also a conversion.
Spiritual meaning: He counted the wound as His own

Look at what the voice asked: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Wait a moment: whom was Saul arresting? Disciples. How could he be persecuting Jesus? But the risen Lord counts the wounds of the church as His own. If you are a brother or sister who has been hurt, please hear this sentence: when someone mistreats you, He is not standing far off watching.
Three: grace has no limit, and someone has to walk the road

1 Timothy has a sentence many of you can recite: “of whom I am chief.” I must be honest: 1 Timothy is one of the disputed letters; many critical scholars think it is not in Paul’s own hand, and many evangelical scholars hold that he wrote it. We do not need to fight that battle here. Even if we look only at the undisputed letters, he says, “I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle.” The meaning is the same.

Notice how he speaks of his past, neither boasting nor hiding. He did not write a book called How I Rose From Persecutor to the Top. Nor did he spend his days in a corner saying he was beyond saving. When he finished speaking of sin, he turned immediately to grace: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” That is what going from self-centered to selfless looks like.
The most concrete shape this grace took in him was a ledger turned over. Listen to how he says it.

However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ. Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ (Philippians 3:7-8)

Picture an accountant moving the items in the asset column one by one into the loss column: bloodline, education, religious record, one item after another. Then he looks up, completely satisfied, and says: the best closing of the books of my life. Brothers and sisters, he did not say these things were fake, and his learning proved useful later. What he said was that these things could no longer serve as his credentials before God. Every one of us has a column we cannot bear to move: my degree, my years of service, the size of my offering, whose son I am. Today it is worth asking yourself: what is that column?

There are two supporting characters in this story that I love. God told Ananias to go to Saul, and Ananias answered immediately: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints.” In plain words: Lord, are you sure you have the right address? Afterward he went anyway, laid his hands on him, and the first words out of his mouth called him “Brother Saul.” Brothers and sisters, those two words are brighter than the light on the Damascus road.

Then Saul came to Jerusalem, and the disciples were all afraid of him, “not believing that he was a disciple.” Perfectly reasonable. At that moment Barnabas stepped forward and took him to the apostles. Without Barnabas, Saul might not even have gotten through that door. The spiritual companions that 235 talks about are people like this.

But I must be careful about one thing. This is not telling people who have been hurt to rush out and embrace the one who hurt them. Grace having no limit does not mean consequences and responsibility disappear; the wounded need boundaries and safety, and that too pleases God. God sending Ananias was His calling for him, not a rule to be used to pressure people.

All of us have a list in our hearts: this person could never come to faith. Perhaps your uncle who rolls his eyes whenever he sees a pastor, perhaps the netizen who scolds Christians online every day. Paul’s story does not guarantee that everyone will change; some people never turn back before they die, and we do not write that kind of check. What it tells us is: do not close the door on God’s behalf.

This week, please write a name on a sheet of paper, the person you think is least likely to believe in Jesus, and pray for him for seven days in a row. That name may even be your own. If you have always felt, what I have done is too terrible, or, I am so rational and so good that I do not need this, Paul went through both of these.

Lord Jesus, You appeared to a man who was persecuting You, and Your grace has no limit. You know all my past; free me from being bound by it, and from boasting in it. Remember the name I have written, and teach me, when You want to send me, to walk that road willingly as Ananias did. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. What similarities or differences are there between Paul’s résumé and your own “testimony”? What do you most easily rely on to feel safe?
2. What do you think of the three explanations of Paul’s experience on the road? If a friend offers a psychological explanation, how would you talk with him without losing respect?
3. Is there an Ananias or a Barnabas in your life? This week, whose Barnabas could you become?
Who Do You Say That I Am?
He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”Peter answered, “You are the Christ.” (Mark 8:29)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today is the last unit of Jesus Hall. We have looked together at the historical sources, the Gospels, His claims, His miracles, the Sermon on the Mount, His character, the cross, the empty tomb, and the disciples and Paul. We also invited the other side onto the stage one by one. If you have walked through all of it, you have investigated more carefully than many people who have sat in church for thirty years. Please give yourselves a round of applause.

Today I will not add another piece of evidence. And let me assure you first: I will not dim the lights, there will be no moving music, I will not ask you to raise your hand, and no one will walk over to your seat and ask whether you have decided. I only want to hand you one question that Jesus Himself asked. You can take this question home with you, and you can think about it for a year.
One: who do people say that I am?

Jesus took His disciples north, to a place about forty kilometers north of the Sea of Galilee called Caesarea Philippi. There was a cave there, a sanctuary for the worship of the god Pan. Herod had built a marble temple nearby, dedicated to the Emperor Augustus. Later his son Philip made the city his capital and named it after Caesar. In other words, this was the “street of religions” of the day: gods on one side, emperors on the other. And it was right near here that He chose to ask.

Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”They told him, “John the Baptizer, and others say Elijah, but others, one of the prophets.” (Mark 8:27-28)
Notice that what people said about Him then was all very high praise. John the Baptizer, Elijah, one of the prophets: these are all good words. It is the same today.

Our Muslim friends respect Him. They call Him Isa, a prophet and messenger of God, born of the virgin Mary, who performed miracles, and the Qur’an even calls Him the Messiah. When they mention His name they often add a blessing. In this respect, some Muslim friends are more reverent than many nominal Christians. But the same book also says that He was only a messenger, and that He was not killed and not crucified.

The Jewish thinker Buber said that from his youth he had seen in Jesus his great brother, but he acknowledged Him as a brother, not as the Messiah. The Dalai Lama, speaking of Jesus, calls Him a spiritually mature, good and warm person, and respects Christians’ understanding of Him. Thich Nhat Hanh values His nonviolence and practice. Gandhi was deeply moved by the Sermon on the Mount, yet did not become a Christian. In Chinese families we also often hear the elders say: Jesus is a good person, all gods deserve respect. There is real goodwill in that sentence.

The respect of these friends is real, and we should thank them. I also want to say clearly that I cite them not to say they secretly approve of Christianity. They do not. The Dalai Lama is not a Christian, and Buber had no intention of converting.
Spiritual meaning: respect is not flattening

But there is something here we cannot pretend not to see. Did Jesus die on the cross? Was He a messenger, or the Lord? These answers cannot all be right at once. A friend shows you a painting; one says it is a landscape, one a portrait, one a forgery. You can respect every one of them, but you cannot pretend they are all talking about the same thing. Real respect is listening seriously until you understand what the other person believes, and neither flattening his faith into my shape nor flattening my faith into his. In Life’s Questions Hall we discussed “Are all religions the same?” and today we will not repeat that.
Two: who do you say that I am?

Then Jesus changed the pronoun. For the previous question, everyone rushed to answer, because reporting other people’s opinions is the easiest thing. This question made the room quiet. Brothers and sisters, we are all very good at “people say.” People say Christianity is Western, people say the Bible contradicts itself, people say the church is full of hypocrites, and some of what people say is not wrong. But Jesus was not asking your coworker, or your grandmother, or even your pastor.

Peter spoke up: “You are the Christ.” Correct! One hundred points! If the story stopped here, he could start writing books. But please keep reading. Jesus went on to say that He must suffer, be killed and rise, and Peter immediately took Him aside to argue with Him. Jesus’ reply was heavy: “Get behind me, Satan!” Full marks on one question, a failing grade on the next, only a few verses apart.
For many friends this is good news. You do not have to understand everything before you begin. Peter at that moment did not even understand what the cross meant, and Jesus did not fire him.

Matthew adds one more line. After Peter answered, Jesus told him that “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Notice that. A person recognizing Jesus does not depend wholly on his brain being good, nor wholly on the preacher’s eloquence; God's own work is in it. So today I do not have to push you hard, and you do not have to feel pushed.

At this, many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him. Jesus said therefore to the twelve, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?”Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. (John 6:66-68)

This passage is also worth looking at. Many walked away, and Jesus did not hold them back, and did not lower the standard to keep numbers. He turned and asked the twelve: “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” The door is open. A place you are free to leave is a place where staying means something.

In the Bible there are people who move at different speeds. Nicodemus was an old scholar who came secretly at night to ask; a few chapters later he quietly said a word of fairness for Jesus; only after Jesus died did he appear openly, bringing myrrh and aloes. He walked a long way, at a slow pace, and Jesus did not hurry him.

There was also a rich young man who came to ask about eternal life. Jesus saw through his heart and said a very hard word, and he “went away sorrowful.” Look at the order Mark writes it in: “Jesus looking at him loved him.” And then? Jesus did not run after him, did not send the disciples to get his phone number, did not say “you’ll regret it if you don’t decide now.” He let him go. He loved him, and He respected him.

When Jesus passed through a Samaritan village and the people did not receive Him, James and John said: “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them?” Jesus turned and rebuked the two disciples, and went on to another village. Brothers and sisters, when we share the gospel we too often carry a little fire. Put it down.
Spiritual meaning: this is not an exam

In asking this question, He does not want a correctly filled-in answer sheet. He wants an encounter. Historical verification can take you to the door, and the door you must open yourself. This is not because the evidence is insufficient, but because the question itself is more than a historical question. If a person walked into your home and asked, “Do you know who I am?”, checking his ID is one thing, and whether to invite him to sit and eat is another.

If someone asks, how do I respond? The New Testament can put it in three words. First, know: who He really is, and what He did. Second, repent: this word does not mean to cry, it means to turn. From “I am the lord of my life” to “You are Lord.” This is the first step from self-centered to selfless. Third, trust: it is like putting your whole weight on a chair. Believing the chair is sturdy is not enough; you have to actually sit down.

For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him. (John 3:16-17)

He did not ask this question in order to condemn you. After asking it, He went on toward Jerusalem. He is the Lord who walked up to the cross and rose from the dead. By the time this question was asked, He had already walked out the answer.
What also must be said honestly

I must also tell you that what Jesus said is not only gentle. He said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” This sentence is very exclusive, many people today are uncomfortable hearing it, and I understand. If His claim is not right, He is not worth following; if His claim is right, He cannot be treated as only one of many good people. We should not edit this sentence out for Him, but please also remember that the One who said it said it before laying down His life for the world. He was not holding a stick when He said it.

For brothers and sisters who already believe, today’s question must still be answered. “You are the Christ” is not something said once on the day of baptism and finished. How does your wallet answer this question? How does your phone’s browsing history answer it? How does the tone you use with your family answer it? Letting Jesus reign is not a slogan. It is answering again every morning.
Now I will give three kinds of friends three different next steps.

The first kind: today you say in your heart, I want to respond. You can pray right now in your own words, or say it silently with me, and I will read it in a moment. Then tell a Christian, start reading the Gospel of John, and find a gathering. The “How to Begin Walking with God” in Life’s Questions Hall of the app can also accompany you through the next few steps.

The second kind: you say, I am not ready yet. Thank you for your honesty. Please finish reading the Gospel of John, write down your questions, and you can also try this prayer: “God, if You are really there, let me know.” God understands that prayer. If your family cares a great deal about ancestor rites and the like, or if where you live there is pressure or even danger in changing faith, please be careful and first talk with someone you trust. Do not take a risk because of a feeling today.

The third kind: you say, I have thought about it, and I do not believe. I truly thank you for listening this far, and you remain a welcome friend here. Christian friends, please listen well too: he is not your sales figure, people matter more than tasks, and your friendship must not change because of his answer. Entrust him to the Holy Spirit, and keep loving him.

Friends who are willing may say along in your heart: Lord Jesus, I believe You died for my sins and rose from the dead. I am willing to turn away from a self-centered life and give my life to You. Forgive me, and be my Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.
That is all for today. No one will come and ask whether you just said it along. His question is still there, waiting for you.
